note: Karten „Reale Geschichte“ (Reich): sachlich, belegt, 450–800 Zeichen, keine Belohnungs- oder Erfolgssprache. NS-Begriffe stehen in Anführungszeichen. Quellen je Karte in data/explore/history_reich.json.

strings.hist.reich.germania.title: Germania: the Great Hall that was never built
strings.hist.reich.germania.text: On 30 January 1937 Hitler appointed Albert Speer General Building Inspector for the Reich capital. By 1950 Berlin was to become the “World Capital Germania”, with a north–south axis some seven kilometres long and 120 metres wide. At its northern end Speer planned the Great Hall: 315 metres along each side, a dome 230 to 250 metres across depending on the source, 290 metres high, around 320 metres with the crowning eagle, with room for 150,000 to 180,000 people. The eagle was to hold the globe in its talons. The hall was never built; the war prevented it. Demolition, however, began as early as 1938, especially in the Alsen quarter by the Reichstag, and went on until 1942. The overall plan would have required more than 50,000 flats to make way. Plans and model photographs survive, for instance from Speer’s papers in the Federal Archives.
strings.hist.reich.evictions.title: Speer’s office and the clearing of Jewish flats
strings.hist.reich.evictions.text: For non-Jewish tenants from houses demolished for Germania, Speer’s office, the General Building Inspector (GBI), found replacements: mostly the flats of Jewish Berliners, whom it forced to move out. The “Law on Tenancies with Jews” of 30 April 1939 had largely removed their protection as tenants. From January 1941 the GBI had thousands of flats cleared in several “actions”; according to the office chronicle, an action to clear some 5,000 Jewish flats began in August 1941. From October 1941 many of those driven out were deported. In 1964 Rudolf Wolters, who had kept the chronicle, had it retyped without the incriminating passages; Speer gave this version to the Federal Archives in 1969. Around 1980 Wolters showed the original to the historian M. Schmidt, whose book exposed the alterations in 1982.
strings.hist.reich.schwerbelastungskoerper.title: The Schwerbelastungskörper: a test load for the triumphal arch
strings.hist.reich.schwerbelastungskoerper.text: In 1941/42 Albert Speer had a concrete cylinder built in Berlin-Tempelhof: 14 metres high, 21 metres in diameter, with foundations some 18 metres deep, weighing about 12,650 tonnes. French forced labourers were among those made to work on it. The structure was meant to simulate the load of the planned triumphal arch on the north–south axis and show whether Berlin’s subsoil could bear it. Soil engineers from the Degebo took measurements until June 1944; the data were not evaluated until 1948. The result: in two and a half years the cylinder had sunk by around 19 centimetres. The arch could only have been built after costly consolidation of the ground. After 1945 the structure served research for decades. In 1995 it was added to Berlin’s list of protected monuments; since 2009 it has been an information site with a viewing platform.
strings.hist.reich.wannsee.title: The Wannsee Protocol: one copy of thirty
strings.hist.reich.wannsee.text: On 20 January 1942, 15 senior representatives of the SS, the NSDAP and Reich ministries, among them their host Reinhard Heydrich, met in a villa on Berlin’s Wannsee. They coordinated the deportation and murder of the Jews of Europe; the protocol’s statistics count some eleven million Jews. Adolf Eichmann wrote the 15-page record. Of 30 copies only one is known: the 16th, intended for Under State Secretary Martin Luther at the Foreign Office. American staff came across it in 1946/47 among the Foreign Office’s recovered files; in March 1947 the document reached the Nuremberg prosecutor Robert Kempner. It entered the judgment of the Ministries Trial; at his trial in Jerusalem in 1961 Eichmann confirmed his authorship. The original is held in the Political Archive of the Federal Foreign Office.
strings.hist.reich.reichsbahn.title: The Reichsbahn files: timetables of deportation
strings.hist.reich.reichsbahn.text: Around three million Jews were deported to ghettos and extermination camps on trains of the Deutsche Reichsbahn. The figure was first calculated by the historian Wolfgang Scheffler, in 1973, as an expert witness at the Düsseldorf trial of Albert Ganzenmüller, once state secretary in the Reich Ministry of Transport. The proceedings were abandoned; after a heart attack Ganzenmüller was deemed unfit to stand trial, and he was never convicted. Timetable orders such as No. 587 record the number of wagons, the arrival time and the train’s next deployment. The fare charged was third class, half the rate for groups of 400 or more, half fare for children under ten, nothing for those under four. The bills went through the Reich Security Main Office. In 1981 Raul Hilberg published such documents in “Sonderzüge nach Auschwitz”.
strings.hist.reich.generalplan_ost.title: Generalplan Ost: what the planning files show
strings.hist.reich.generalplan_ost.text: From 1939/40 Himmler had plans drawn up for the “Germanisation” of Eastern Europe. The Reich Security Main Office’s version from late 1941 is lost, but is known from a statement by Erhard Wetzel of the Ministry for the East dated 27 April 1942: of 45 million “alien peoples”, 31 million were to be “resettled” to Western Siberia; Wetzel even arrived at 46 to 51 million. A “resettlement” of the Jews “becomes unnecessary”, he wrote, “with the solution of the Jewish question”. The Nuremberg document NG-2325 appeared in print in 1958. Konrad Meyer’s version of June 1942 survives: almost five million German settlers in 25 years. The murder of the Jews was taken as given; millions more deaths were factored in. In 1948 Meyer was convicted only of SS membership; in 1956 he became a professor in Hanover.
strings.hist.reich.t4.title: Aktion T4: the Hartheim statistics
strings.hist.reich.t4.text: From January 1940 patients from mental hospitals and care homes were murdered with gas in six killing centres, directed from Tiergartenstraße 4 in Berlin. In 1945 American soldiers found an internal tally at Hartheim near Linz: “Disinfected up to 1 September 1941: persons: 70,273”. It became a principal source for the number of victims in this phase. After the gassings were stopped in August 1941, the killing continued in a decentralised way: through starvation, neglect, drugs. Researchers estimate 250,000 to 300,000 victims across Europe. The Nuremberg Doctors’ Trial, which also dealt with these murders, ended in 1947 with seven death sentences; only a few perpetrators were ever called to account. In 1990 some 30,000 patient files turned up in the former Stasi archive. In 2025 the Bundestag recognised the victims as persecuted by the Nazi regime.
strings.hist.reich.forced_labor.title: Forced labour in the Reich and the late compensation
strings.hist.reich.forced_labor.text: Over 13 million civilians, prisoners of war and concentration camp prisoners were forced to work in the German Reich between 1939 and 1945; at the end of 1944 more than 7.5 million foreign workers were employed there. People from Poland and the Soviet Union had to wear a “P” or “OST”; many lived in barracks and went hungry. After 1945 most received nothing: the Federal Compensation Act largely excluded those living abroad, and the London Debt Agreement deferred their claims as a reparations matter. After class actions in the USA, the foundation “Remembrance, Responsibility and Future” was set up in August 2000 with DM 10.1 billion from the federal government and industry. By 2007, 1.66 million survivors or heirs in 98 countries had received 4.4 billion euros. Prisoners of war who had not been held in concentration camps remained excluded.
